# Command reference

Every command the shipped build dispatches, every parameter it declares, and — for most —
a real captured session. Nothing on this page is hand-written: the descriptions come from the
same `meta.params` that generates `dot --help`, and each example was **executed** against a
throwaway repository at build time. What you see under `$ dot …` is what the CLI actually printed.

The examples run in order against one small source, so later outputs depend on earlier
calls. The repository is a four-file handbook:

- `notes/retention.md`
- `notes/deletion-runbook.md`
- `notes/onboarding.md`
- `decisions/2026-02-adopt-postgres.md`

A few examples show a **refusal** rather than a success. Those are marked, and they are
there on purpose: what going wrong looks like is part of the interface.

## Reading a result

Every command answers with the same envelope — `{ "ok": true, "result": … }` or
`{ "ok": false, "error": …, "code": … }`. Advisory notes (which tree answered, what was
inferred) go to **stderr**, so piping stdout to `jq` stays clean.

A field shown as `"<varies>"` was **redacted, not invented**: build stamps, timestamps and
the staleness scores `search_triage` ranks on change between any two runs, so pinning them
to a plausible-looking number would print a value that is true for nobody. Everything else
on this page is verbatim.

## `comms_read`

Read comms addressed to `as` (`to === as` or `to === 'all'`), oldest first. With `since` omitted (the common case) this resumes from a persisted per-reader cursor and ADVANCES it to the last message returned before returning — each message is delivered to a given `as` exactly once across calls, not re-scanned on every poll. Pass `since` explicitly to replay from an earlier point instead; an explicit `since` never touches the stored cursor. On a default call the response's own `since` is the point the next default call would resume from — but on an explicit-`since` call the response's `since` is just your input echoed back, not the persisted cursor; call `comms_read` with `since` omitted to learn the persisted cursor.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL. Omitted, dotworld infers it from your working directory (your own workspace counts), exactly like every other command's sourceId. |
| `as` | string | yes | the mailbox to read as — matches messages sent `to` this name or to 'all', and names the persisted cursor. |
| `since` | number |  | OPTIONAL — replay strictly after this sequence number instead of the stored cursor. Does not advance or read the stored cursor. |

```console
$ dot comms_read as=bob
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "messages": [
      {
        "seq": 1,
        "at": "<varies>",
        "from": "alice",
        "to": "bob",
        "topic": "retention",
        "body": "Incident note is in. The `purge` job needs a runbook line about the skipped night."
      }
    ],
    "since": "<varies>"
  }
}
```

## `comms_send`

Append one message to the source-wide comms log — cross-workspace messaging between sibling `workspace_open` agents on the same source. Not durable knowledge: this is scratch coordination, disposable like the rest of `.dotworld/derived/`, never a substitute for landing real work through `workspace_submit`. Every worktree of the source sees every message — storage is rooted at the source, not your own workspace.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL. Omitted, dotworld infers it from your working directory (your own workspace counts), exactly like every other command's sourceId. |
| `from` | string | yes | the sender's own name — there is no reliable identity to infer this from, so name yourself explicitly, the same string every time. |
| `to` | string | yes | the recipient's name, or 'all' to broadcast to every reader. |
| `topic` | string | yes | a short subject line. |
| `body` | string | yes | the message body. |

The body is data. It is passed as an argv element, never through a shell, so backticks in it stay backticks.

```console
$ dot comms_send from=alice to=bob topic=retention 'body=Incident note is in. The `purge` job needs a runbook line about the skipped night.'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "ok": true,
    "seq": 1,
    "at": "<varies>"
  }
}
```

## `context_load`

Load a `files`/`index` list as one prompt-ready blob — a dynamic alternative to a static CLAUDE.md/agent-definition file: point `index` at a document and edit that document to change what loads next time, no redeploy. `mode=file` joins full file bodies (`file_read`); `mode=dot` joins each dot (`dot_get`) — title, tags, summary, authored body. Same resolution as those two commands: `files`, `index`, or both (index appended after files, deduped) — naming neither refuses. `entries` carries the raw per-file rows (exactly what `file_read`/`dot_get` would answer) for a caller that wants to filter or reorder; `context` is the same information already joined into one string, in resolution order, ready to drop into a prompt. `missing` names anything that did not resolve (not found, or a dot that could not be parsed) — never a refusal. `mode=file` also reports `binary`: file paths whose bytes are not text, skipped from the blob rather than lossily decoded, exactly like `file_read`. Adds nothing `file_read`/`dot_get` do not already compute — a formatting convenience over their output, never a third source of truth.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL. Omitted, dotworld infers it from your working directory (your own workspace counts), exactly like every other command's sourceId. |
| `files` | array of string |  | file paths or ids to load — use instead of (or as well as) `index`. Over the CLI this is CWD-relative, exactly like `git add`; MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root. |
| `index` | string |  | a document whose LINKS are the list of files to load — use instead of (or as well as) `files`. Any document works: a generated index from `index_create`, or a hand-written note with links in prose. Read from the file every call, so pruning a line changes the answer, exactly like `file_read index=`/`dot_get index=`. |
| `mode` | string | yes | 'file' loads full file bodies (what `file_read` returns) — the raw content, byte for byte. 'dot' loads each file's dot (what `dot_get` returns) — title, tags, summary and authored body, without the file body itself. Pick `file` when the files themselves are the context (source, specs); pick `dot` when a lighter summary of many files is enough. No default — the two answers differ enough that guessing one would silently pick a context budget for you. |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from (default: the canonical checkout — see `file_read`'s `workspace` param, which this matches exactly). |

```console
$ dot context_load index=notes/retention-pack.md mode=dot
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "mode": "dot",
    "entries": [
      {
        "id": "notes/retention.md",
        "path": "notes/retention.md",
        "title": "Data retention policy",
        "tags": [
          "policy",
          "compliance"
        ],
        "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->",
        "centrality": 0.2242466713385889,
        "obsolete": false,
        "kind": "prose",
        "owner": "alice",
        "body": "Reviewed each quarter by the data protection lead.\n",
        "summaryStatus": "unread"
      },
      {
        "id": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",
        "path": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",
        "title": "Deletion runbook",
        "tags": [],
        "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->",
        "centrality": 0.3255080588644246,
        "obsolete": false,
        "kind": "prose",
… 22 more lines of output
```

## `dot_attach`

Attach a STRANDED dot to a file — the manual half of rename reconciliation, for the move it could not pair. It RELOCATES one dot; it does not relate two things, and it authors no edge — `graph_connect` is that command. Both params name FILES, never `.dot.md` paths: `dot` is the path the stranded dot still describes (as `dot_list orphaned=true` reports it), `file` is the file to attach it to. This does everything a detected rename does — rewrites the dot's `id` and `source_path`, moves the dot, and rewrites authored connectors naming the old path — which is why hand-moving the `.dot.md` is NOT equivalent: that silently severs every curated edge. Nothing is merged: the dot you name wins outright, because the reason you are here is that automatic pairing already guessed wrong once. FOUR REFUSALS. (1) The named dot's own file still exists — nothing is stranded; move the file instead and the next read carries its dot. (2) `file` is not a file in this working tree. (3) The destination already has an AUTHORED dot — pass overwrite=true to replace it; a BLANK one, such as the one an interim read minted at the new path, is replaced without asking. A TITLE COUNTS as authored when dotworld did not mint it (a minted one is the filename stem or the file's own first H1), so a destination carrying nothing but a title somebody wrote is refused like any other; the refusal names it, and overwrite is all-or-nothing, so re-author it with `dot_set` afterwards if you wanted it kept. (4) Either dot is unparseable. The two halves of (4) differ, deliberately: a defective dot at the DESTINATION is replaceable with overwrite=true, because it is being discarded wholesale, but a defective dot at `dot` is refused outright and overwrite=true will not clear it — its `id` and `source_path` cannot be rewritten without reading it, so moving it would leave a broken dot describing a different file. Repair that one by hand first; the refusal names the repair.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `dot` | string | yes | the file path the stranded dot describes (NOT the .dot.md path) |
| `file` | string | yes | the file to attach that dot to |
| `overwrite` | boolean |  | replace an authored (or unparseable) dot at the destination (default false) |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

The manual half of rename reconciliation. `dot` is the path the stranded dot DESCRIBES, not the `.dot.md` path.

```console
$ dot dot_attach dot=notes/deletion-runbook.md file=notes/purge-runbook.md
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "from": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",
    "to": "notes/purge-runbook.md",
    "replaced": "blank",
    "connectors": 0
  }
}
```

## `dot_get`

READ A FILE'S DOT — the whole dot by default, or named components via `fields`. A dot carries title, tags, properties and an authorable body; the answer adds derived signals (centrality, summaryStatus). `centrality` is PageRank over the connector graph with `supersedes` edges LEFT OUT (#324) — an edge recording that a document is dead is not evidence it matters — so a superseded file ranks on its other links alone. This is the TRIAGE step: it tells you whether a file is worth opening without paying for the FILE's body (that is `file_read`). The DOT body IS included by default — it is authored scratch notes about the file and is usually empty, so it costs nothing like `file_read`; `fields=["body"]` reads it alone. Name the files with `files`, or point `index` at a document and every file IT LINKS TO is the list. Addressed by the FILE's path: identity is the path, and a dot is never addressed by its own. `dot_set` is the matching writer. FOR PROPERTIES, PREFER `property_get`: this command's projection OMITS a field the dot does not carry, so an absent property is indistinguishable from one you did not ask for — `property_get` names it in `missing` instead. `properties` is the trap, because it is not a field at all: property keys are spread at the TOP LEVEL of the answer, so `fields=["properties"]` answers `{"path":"…"}` for every file, always — name the property KEYS you want.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `files` | array of string |  | file paths or ids. Over the CLI this is CWD-relative, exactly like `git add` — MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root (#337). |
| `index` | string |  | a document whose LINKS are the list of files — use instead of (or as well as) `files`. Any document works, not a special format: a generated index from `index_create`, or a hand-written note with links in prose. Read from the file every time, so pruning a line changes the answer. External URLs and dead links are skipped rather than reported missing. Over the CLI this is CWD-RELATIVE, exactly like git (#337); MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root. |
| `fields` | array of string |  | return only these components — e.g. ["body"], ["tags","summary"], or any property key. Omit for the whole dot. `path` is always present, and asking for `summary` always brings `summaryStatus` with it. |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

```console
$ dot dot_get 'files=["notes/retention.md"]'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": [
    {
      "id": "notes/retention.md",
      "path": "notes/retention.md",
      "title": "Data retention policy",
      "tags": [],
      "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->",
      "centrality": 0.28804982483429553,
      "obsolete": false,
      "kind": "prose",
      "body": "",
      "summaryStatus": "unread"
    }
  ]
}

ANSWERED FROM THE CANONICAL CHECKOUT — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```

## `dot_list`

Every dot in this source as an OBJECT: the file it describes, where the `.dot.md` itself lives, and whether that file is still here. `orphaned=true` is the one that matters — a dot whose file is ABSENT from the working tree. An orphan is durable, in git, and holds real authored metadata, and nothing else in the command set can see it: `file_tree` lists files, and every aggregate over dots (`search_properties`, `property_list` counts) is computed over live files only, so a property that exists solely on an orphan reads as used by nobody. TWO WAYS A DOT IS ORPHANED, and the second is the common one: a file DELETED on purpose leaves its dot behind (retire it with `git rm` of the `dotPath` here), and a file MOVED out of band leaves it behind when reconciliation could not pair the two halves (reattach it with `dot_attach`) — see `sync_source`. An orphan row carries the metadata stranded on it, so you can judge whether it is worth recovering without opening anything, plus `hint`/`hintReason`: where the file probably went, ADVISORY and NEVER acted on. Weigh the three reasons differently — `git-rename-in-the-deleting-commit` is git's own pairing of the two paths; `closest-embedding` is the nearest of that commit's arrivals to the orphan's last committed content in vector space, carrying `hintScore` (cosine, 0-1), which is how you tell a continuation from a coincidence; `the-only-file-added-in-that-commit` is mere co-occurrence: `git rm obsolete.md`, add `CHANGELOG.md`, commit, and the changelog is hinted, with nothing whatever to do with the file that left — and its `hintScore`, when present, is what says so. A near-tie gives NO `hint` and a `hintTie` listing the candidates with their scores instead, because naming one would be a coin toss dressed as evidence. `semanticHints` says whether the embedding hint ran at all: on the model-free `hashing` fallback it declines, because cosine over that engine is noise — ask `embedding_info` why the real model is not running. `orphaned` counts the stranded dots whether or not you filtered for them, so a plain call answers "is anything stranded?" in one go. THE SECOND STATE IS `indexed`, and it is a different condition with a different repair: a file that IS here (`exists: true`) yet is outside what this source tracks — which is what a file that acquired a dot and was then GITIGNORED looks like. Its metadata is invisible to every query for the same reason an orphan's is, so `notIndexedReason` says why and `ignoredBy` names the rule as git names it: the ignore FILE, the LINE and the PATTERN. The repair is to change that rule or move the file, and it is NEITHER orphan repair — nothing is stranded, `dot_attach` has nothing to reattach, and `git rm` would throw the metadata away. `notIndexed` is counted separately from `orphaned` for exactly that reason, and is likewise reported whether or not you filtered.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `orphaned` | boolean |  | only dots whose file is absent from this working tree (default false: every dot) |
| `notIndexed` | boolean |  | only dots whose file IS in this working tree and is not indexed — gitignored, usually (default false: every dot). Disjoint from `orphaned`, which selects dots with no file at all, so asking for both returns no rows; both counts report either way |
| `match` | string |  | case-insensitive substring of the FILE PATH the dot describes. This queries paths — `search_properties` is how you query property values |
| `limit` | number |  | maximum rows (default 200; negative for no limit). A source has one dot per file, so an unbounded call on a large one returns a row per file; `truncated: true` says the answer was cut short, and `total` says by how much |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

```console
$ dot dot_list limit=3
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "total": 4,
    "orphaned": 0,
    "notIndexed": 0,
    "returned": 3,
    "truncated": true,
    "dots": [
      {
        "path": "decisions/2026-02-adopt-postgres.md",
        "dotPath": ".dotworld/dots/decisions/2026-02-adopt-postgres.md.dot.md",
        "exists": true,
        "indexed": true
      },
      {
        "path": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",
        "dotPath": ".dotworld/dots/notes/deletion-runbook.md.dot.md",
        "exists": true,
        "indexed": true
      },
      {
        "path": "notes/onboarding.md",
        "dotPath": ".dotworld/dots/notes/onboarding.md.dot.md",
        "exists": true,
        "indexed": true
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

A dot whose file is gone and whose rename could not be resolved is STRANDED. The old runbook was deleted and recreated under a new name in a separate commit, so git had no rename to detect — its title, tags and properties are still here, attached to nothing.

```console
$ dot dot_list orphaned=true
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "total": 1,
    "orphaned": 1,
    "notIndexed": 0,
    "returned": 1,
    "truncated": false,
    "dots": [
      {
        "path": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",
        "dotPath": ".dotworld/dots/notes/deletion-runbook.md.dot.md",
        "exists": false,
        "indexed": false,
        "title": "Deletion runbook",
        "tags": [],
        "properties": {
          "kind": "prose",
          "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->"
        }
… 8 more lines of output
```

Nothing stranded any more.

```console
$ dot dot_list orphaned=true
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "total": 0,
    "orphaned": 0,
    "notIndexed": 0,
    "returned": 0,
    "truncated": false,
    "dots": []
  }
}
```

## `dot_set`

WRITE A FILE'S DOT — the matching setter for `dot_get`, and the only VALIDATED way to change a `title` or `tags` once a file exists (`file_create` sets them at birth; `property_set` refuses them, because writing one through a property bag overwrote the real field). Name the components you want written: `title`, `tags`, `body`, `properties`. A COMPONENT YOU OMIT IS LEFT ALONE, never cleared, and `properties` names the keys to write rather than replacing the whole bag — so a narrow edit cannot silently discard metadata you did not mention. The SOURCE FILE is never touched: metadata lives in the dot (use `file_create` to write file content). THE DOT IS DURABLE AND IN GIT, so the edit only survives once it is committed — dotworld never commits for you (#370), in a workspace or the shared checkout alike: this writes the dot and leaves it uncommitted for you to land with `git` — a dot that never lands is invisible to every clone. `workspace_submit` refuses to land a workspace with uncommitted changes, naming them. `properties` is held to the SAME registry check as `property_set` — an unregistered key is refused, and the whole write is refused with it rather than half-applied. `title` and `tags` need no registration; they are not properties.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `file` | string | yes | file path or id — the FILE's path, as everywhere: a dot is never addressed by its own |
| `title` | string |  | replace the dot title |
| `tags` | array of string |  | replace the tag list outright (this is an authored edit, not a merge) |
| `body` | string |  | replace the dot's authorable body outright — freeform notes ABOUT the file (working notes, open questions, why-this-is-weird), never the file's own content. Within your tree this REPLACES what is there (an authored edit, not a merge), so read it first if you mean to add to it. ACROSS a divergence it is different: the body merges by line-union and never conflicts, so a note another writer added concurrently is kept beside yours. Five things that surprise callers. Their lines are RELOCATED to the end of the changed region, so a note written above a shared line can come out below it, and the merge is not commutative — two people merging the same branches can get different, both-valid bodies. Nothing is inserted at the JUNCTION between your lines and theirs — each writer's own blank lines survive, but neither wrote one there, so two stanzas can abut. Removing a line removes that COPY, but lines are matched by TEXT: if the other writer authored a line with the same text, one survives. A line you both edited appears TWICE, once each. And it merges BY LINE with no knowledge of markup, so a fenced code block you both edit can interleave — keep a note on its own line. Standing guidance that should outlive a session belongs in the `agent_instructions` property. |
| `properties` | object |  | property keys to write; each must be registered (see property_register) |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

```console
$ dot dot_set file=notes/retention.md 'title=Data retention policy' 'tags=["policy","compliance"]' 'body=Reviewed each quarter by the data protection lead.'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "path": "notes/retention.md",
    "title": "Data retention policy",
    "tags": [
      "policy",
      "compliance"
    ],
    "properties": {
      "kind": "prose",
      "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->"
    },
    "body": "Reviewed each quarter by the data protection lead.\n"
  }
}
```

## `embedding_info`

The active semantic-search model, and whether it is the one that was configured. Returns { engine, dim, quality, available, requested, honored, reason, note, configFile, build, maxTokens }. `quality` is the one field that answers "is search healthy right now" — 'ok' or a 'degraded-…' value — and it is keyed on the LIVE engine, not on `reason` alone: `reason` says why a REQUEST was disobeyed ('unknown-engine' — bad name or a stale build; 'construct-failed' — package/weights missing; 'auto-fallback' — `auto` found no real engine), so `requested: null, honored: true, reason: null` was byte-identical whether no engine was ever configured OR a real dotworld.config.json simply was not found from this cwd (config discovery is cwd-sensitive, docs/plugins.md) — both landed on the built-in `hashing` fallback while reading as healthy. `quality: 'degraded-no-config'` names exactly that state (#353). `configFile` names which file (if any) produced this answer, and `note` says so in prose. `maxTokens` (null when the engine has no such ceiling) is how many tokens of a document the model actually sees — a file longer than that is ranked on its opening section only, with everything past it silently unseen (#355). When degraded, prefer search_grep for exact identifiers and open more candidates than usual. This is about EMBEDDINGS only: for the build stamp, the node version and the command set ask `version`, and for whether the install is healthy at all ask `sync_doctor`.

_No parameters._

```console
$ dot embedding_info
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "engine": "fastembed",
    "dim": 384,
    "quality": "ok",
    "available": [
      "hashing",
      "fastembed"
    ],
    "requested": "fastembed",
    "honored": true,
    "reason": null,
```

## `file_create`

Create or overwrite a FILE, and mint its DOT in the same act. Two artifacts, and the split is the whole model: the file at `path` holds the content and stays RAW — no frontmatter is ever written into it — while `title`, `tags` and `properties` land on the dot beside it at `.dotworld/dots/<path>.dot.md`. A file committed without its dot is invisible to every clone, which is why this writes both. REFUSES a `content` write to a path whose bytes on disk are BINARY (#327): `content` is a string, so the write would replace an image or archive with its utf8 decode. Delete such a file first to replace it with text on purpose, or change its bytes yourself and stage them with `git`. DOTWORLD NEVER COMMITS (#370): this writes the file and its dot to disk and nothing more — staging and committing are yours, with `git` (subcommand=add, then subcommand=commit) or your own shell. `workspace_submit` refuses to land a workspace with uncommitted changes, naming them, rather than silently reporting success over work still sitting on disk.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `path` | string | yes | source-relative path |
| `content` | string |  | source file content |
| `title` | string |  | title (else derived from H1/filename). `dot_set` changes it later |
| `tags` | array of string |  | tags — must be strings. `dot_set` changes them later |
| `properties` | object |  | dot properties. Each key must be REGISTERED (see `property_register`) and may not be reserved dot frontmatter — use the `title`/`tags` params above, not the bag, which would overwrite the dot's real field. A refused write leaves NO file behind. |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

Creates the file and mints its dot in one act — no `sync_source` needed afterwards.

```console
$ dot file_create path=notes/incident-2026-03.md 'content=# Incident: purge job skipped a night

The nightly purge did not run on 2026-03-11. Logs older than 90 days
survived one extra day. No customer data left the system.
' 'title=Incident: purge job skipped a night' 'tags=["incident"]'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "id": "notes/incident-2026-03.md",
    "sourceId": "handbook",
    "path": "notes/incident-2026-03.md",
    "title": "Incident: purge job skipped a night",
    "tags": [
      "incident"
    ],
    "dot": {
      "id": "notes/incident-2026-03.md",
      "source_id": "handbook",
      "title": "Incident: purge job skipped a night",
      "tags": [
        "incident"
      ],
      "source_path": "$DOTWORLD_ROOT/notes/incident-2026-03.md",
      "properties": {
        "kind": "prose",
        "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->"
      },
      "body": ""
    }
  }
}
```

## `file_delete`

Remove a FILE and its DOT as one act — the inverse of `file_create`. Exactly two things are deleted, and that pairing is the unit: a file removed without its `.dot.md` leaves an ORPHAN, durable metadata describing nothing, which is the case `dot_list orphaned=true` exists to make findable — so this never creates one. Identity is the path, which is why there is no separate retire verb: naming a path whose file is ALREADY GONE retires its stranded dot, and that is how you clear an orphan you decided not to reattach. THE DOT GOES WITH THE FILE, NO SEPARATE CONFIRMATION: whatever it held — tags, properties, a body, a hand-written title — is deleted along with the file it describes; naming the file is the instruction for both. REFERENCES ARE REPORTED, NOT REMOVED AND NOT A REFUSAL: authored connectors naming this path are kept on purpose (an edge outliving its endpoint is how provenance works, so a `supersedes` edge pointing here still answers `graph_provenance` — use `graph_disconnect` if you want one gone), and `referencedBy` names the files whose own TEXT links here, which dotworld does not edit because a wikilink is bytes in somebody's document. Refused on a tree with unmerged paths, exactly as `file_create` is — and REFUSED WHEN GIT DOES NOT HOLD THE FILE'S CURRENT BYTES: untracked, ignored, or modified since the last commit, because then this is the only copy and nothing could bring it back. Commit it first and the delete is recoverable from history, or pass force=true — that gate covers the FILE, and the dot rides along with whatever it decides. DOTWORLD NEVER COMMITS (#370): this removes the file and its dot from disk and nothing more — staging and committing are yours, with `git` or your own shell. `workspace_submit` refuses to land a workspace with uncommitted changes, naming them, rather than silently reporting success over work still sitting on disk.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `path` | string | yes | source-relative path of the file to delete |
| `force` | boolean |  | delete the file even though git does not hold its current bytes (default false). This is the unrecoverable case and the only one, so the refusal names which of untracked, ignored or modified it hit; a clean tracked file never needs this |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

Removes the file and its dot as one act — the inverse of `file_create`.

```console
$ dot file_delete path=notes/incident-2026-03.md force=true
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "path": "notes/incident-2026-03.md",
    "removed": true,
    "dotRemoved": true,
    "connectors": [],
    "referencedBy": [
      "notes/retention-pack.md"
    ],
    "detail": "notes/retention-pack.md still links to notes/incident-2026-03.md in its own text. That link is now dead, and dotworld did not edit it: a wikilink is bytes in somebody's document, so removing one is an authored change (`file_create`)."
  }
}
```

## `file_read`

Retrieval (lazy): file bodies for the few files that matter. A row with `content` is the file byte for byte and is authoritative. TWO rows carry no body. `binary: true` means the file is not text (a NUL byte in its first 8000 — git's own test), so `content` is OMITTED rather than utf8-decoded: the decode would give you U+FFFD where the bytes were, and writing that back destroys the file, so `file_create`/`file_stage` refuse such a path. Read what dotworld knows about it with `dot_get` instead, and change its bytes with `git`. `dotUnparseable: true` is the opposite case — the FILE read fine and only its dot could not be parsed.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `files` | array of string |  | file paths or ids. Over the CLI this is CWD-relative, exactly like `git add` — MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root (#337). |
| `index` | string |  | a document whose LINKS are the list of files — use instead of (or as well as) `files`. Any document works, not a special format: a generated index from `index_create`, or a hand-written note with links in prose. Read from the file every time, so pruning a line changes the answer. External URLs and dead links are skipped rather than reported missing. Over the CLI this is CWD-RELATIVE, exactly like git (#337); MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root. |
| `ranges` | object |  | optional { file: [start,end] } line ranges |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

```console
$ dot file_read 'files=["notes/retention.md"]'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": [
    {
      "path": "notes/retention.md",
      "content": "# Data retention policy\n\nWe keep customer event logs for 90 days, then delete them. Billing records are\nkept for seven years, because the tax authority can ask for them that far back.\n\nDeletion is a hard delete, not a flag: see [[notes/deletion-runbook.md]].\n"
    }
  ]
}

ANSWERED FROM THE CANONICAL CHECKOUT — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```

The conflicted file, markers and all. Read it before you settle it.

```console
$ dot file_read 'files=["notes/retention.md"]'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": [
    {
      "path": "notes/retention.md",
      "content": "# Data retention policy\n\n<<<<<<< HEAD\nWe keep customer event logs for 180 days, then delete them. Billing records are\n=======\nWe keep customer event logs for 30 days, then delete them. Billing records are\n>>>>>>> e281999 (retention: shorten the log window to 30 days)\nkept for seven years, because the tax authority can ask for them that far back.\n\nDeletion is a hard delete, not a flag: see [[notes/deletion-runbook.md]].\n"
    }
  ]
}

ANSWERED FROM THE WORKSPACE /path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```

## `file_stage`

Finish a conflicted file: write your reconciled text for ONE path that git currently reports as unmerged, and stage it. Does NOT commit — you commit with the `git` command, which is what keeps `rebase --continue` / `merge --continue` working. This is the step between reading a conflicted file (`file_read`) and continuing the rebase: without it you can see a collision and not answer it. NOT a general file write and NOT how you author: it refuses any path git does not report as unmerged, and it never touches the file's dot. Use `file_create` to author (it materialises the dot; a file landed without its .dot.md is invisible to every clone). Content still containing conflict markers is refused — send the reconciled text, not the marked block. So is a path whose bytes on disk are BINARY (#327): this command writes a string, and a conflicted image is settled with `git checkout --ours`/`--theirs` and `git add`, not with reconciled text.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `path` | string | yes | the unmerged source-relative path |
| `content` | string | yes | the reconciled file content, markers removed |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

Write the reconciled text for ONE conflicted path. This is how a conflict ends — dotworld never picks a side, and never hands you a per-field payload to answer.

```console
$ dot file_stage path=notes/retention.md 'content=# Data retention policy

We keep customer event logs for 90 days, then delete them. Billing records are
kept for seven years, because the tax authority can ask for them that far back.

Deletion is a hard delete, not a flag: see [[notes/deletion-runbook.md]].
'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "path": "notes/retention.md",
    "tree": "/path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob",
    "staged": true,
    "committed": false
  }
}
```

## `git`

Run git in your working tree. THIS IS GIT, not a dotworld abstraction: the subcommands mean exactly what they mean in a shell, and the output is git's own. Use it to see a conflict (status, diff), resolve just the marked region and carry on (add, then rebase --continue / merge --continue), or inspect history (log, show). A non-zero exitCode is a normal answer, not a failure — a conflicted merge or rebase is LEFT IN PLACE for you to edit, with the conflicted paths in `unmerged` and their diff in `diff`. Only an allowlisted set is available; anything else is refused with BAD_PARAMS. THIS IS ALSO HOW YOU SEE ANOTHER AGENT AT WORK: pass their workspace path (from `workspace_list`) as `workspace` and `status`/`diff`/`log` answer about THEIR tree, including work they have not committed — the `tree` field says which tree answered. And because linked worktrees share one repository, their branch is an ordinary ref from anywhere: `ref=users/<name>` with `log`/`diff` to read it, with `merge`/`rebase` to build on it while they are still working. Nothing has to be landed first. An untracked `.dot.md` colliding with what `subcommand=rebase` would touch is never cleared out of the way — a read never mints one, so if one is there it is real, uncommitted work, and git refuses the whole rebase over it exactly as it would for any other untracked collision; commit it first.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `subcommand` | string | yes | git subcommand — one of: add, branch, commit, diff, log, merge, rebase, restore, show, status |
| `paths` | array of string |  | working-tree-relative paths (never escaping the tree). Over the CLI this is CWD-relative, exactly like plain `git` — MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root (#337). The bare source root (e.g. `.`) is a valid pathspec, same as `git add .`. |
| `ref` | string |  | branch, tag or revision (may not begin with "-") |
| `message` | string |  | commit / merge message |
| `flags` | array of string |  | per-subcommand allowlisted flags, e.g. --porcelain, --continue, --abort |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

```console
$ dot git subcommand=status
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "subcommand": "status",
    "args": [
      "--no-pager",
      "status"
    ],
    "tree": "/path/to/handbook",
    "exitCode": 0,
    "stdout": "On branch main\nUntracked files:\n  (use \"git add <file>...\" to include in what will be committed)\n\t.dotworld/connectors/\n\t.dotworld/dots/\n\t.dotworld/properties.json\n\t.dotworld/publish-policy.json\n\tnotes/incident-2026-03.md\n\tnotes/retention-pack.md\n\nnothing added to commit but untracked files present (use \"git add\" to track)\n",
    "stderr": ""
  }
}
```

dotworld never commits on your behalf. Stage the dots alongside the files they describe — `.dotworld/dots/` is durable and belongs in the same commit as the source change.

```console
$ dot git subcommand=add 'paths=["."]'
```

## `graph_connect`

Author an explicit connector (incl. supersedes provenance edges). Authoring one over a pair the body text already links gives ONE edge carrying your type and weight, not two counted twice.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `from` | string | yes | from file path |
| `to` | string | yes | to file path |
| `type` | string |  | connector type (default links) |
| `weight` | number |  | weight (default 1). A PROPORTION, not an amount: it says how this file splits its own rank across its out-edges, so scaling every out-edge of one file changes nothing. Must be finite and greater than 0 — it divides into PageRank centrality and sums into `search_triage` ranking, so a non-finite weight would NaN those scores for the whole source. A small fraction says this edge counts for little; `graph_disconnect`, not `weight=0`, says it counts for nothing. |
| `properties` | object |  | connector properties |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

```console
$ dot graph_connect from=notes/incident-2026-03.md to=notes/deletion-runbook.md type=links
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "id": "links:notes/incident-2026-03.md->notes/deletion-runbook.md",
    "sourceId": "handbook",
    "from": "notes/incident-2026-03.md",
    "to": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",
    "type": "links",
    "weight": 1,
    "properties": {},
    "derived": false
  }
}
```

`supersedes` is a provenance edge — it records that one file replaced another, which is what `graph_provenance` reads.

```console
$ dot graph_connect from=notes/retention.md to=decisions/2026-02-adopt-postgres.md type=supersedes
{
  "ok": true,

    "id": "supersedes:notes/retention.md->decisions/2026-02-adopt-postgres.md",
    "sourceId": "handbook",
    "from": "notes/retention.md",
    "to": "decisions/2026-02-adopt-postgres.md",
    "type": "supersedes",
    "weight": 1,
    "properties": {},
```

## `graph_disconnect`

Remove an AUTHORED connector — the inverse of `graph_connect`. Name the same `from`, `to` and `type` you connected with (`type` defaults to 'links', so a `supersedes` edge must be named as one). Authored connectors are the only ones this touches: an edge that comes from a `[[wikilink]]` or a markdown link in a file's BODY is derived, recomputed from the text on every read, and is refused here — removing it means editing that document with `file_create`, and nothing else would make it stick. When BOTH exist over the same pair, the authored one is removed and `derivedEdgeRemains: true` says the edge will still be in `graph_get`, so you are not left thinking the command did nothing.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `from` | string | yes | from file path |
| `to` | string | yes | to file path |
| `type` | string |  | connector type (default links) — must match the one you connected with |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

```console
$ dot graph_disconnect from=notes/incident-2026-03.md to=notes/deletion-runbook.md type=links
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "removed": true,

    "from": "notes/incident-2026-03.md",
    "to": "notes/deletion-runbook.md",

    "derivedEdgeRemains": false
```

## `graph_get`

Analysis: the connector structure around seed files. Returns { seeds, nodes, edges }. Each node carries `hop` (0 = a seed) and `via` ({from, edgeType}) saying how it was reached, so the result reads as an ordered list rather than a topology you must re-derive; `superseded: true` marks a file something supersedes — do not read it as current. A `supersedes` edge is also the one type importance ignores (#324), so an edge visible here contributes nothing to the `centrality` reported by `dot_get` and `search_triage`. `expanded` is true when ALL of that node's connectors (under the filters you asked for) are in this response, false when it sat on the cut, with `unexpandedEdges` counting what was not followed — so "no edges" never has to be guessed at. Re-query with that node as a seed to continue. Narrow with `direction`/`edgeTypes` before reaching for more hops: one filtered hop answers most questions.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `files` | array of string | yes | seed file paths or ids |
| `hops` | number |  | hops to expand from the seeds (default 1); 0 returns the seeds alone, unexpanded |
| `depth` | number |  | deprecated alias for `hops` — same meaning, kept for one release |
| `direction` | string |  | 'out' = what the seeds point at · 'in' = what points at them · 'both' (default). Any other value is refused with BAD_PARAMS rather than silently treated as 'both' |
| `edgeTypes` | array of string |  | restrict the walk to these connector types, e.g. ['supersedes'] to follow provenance only |
| `limit` | number |  | max nodes to return, nearest-first — LOSSY, so a set question ("everything that supersedes this") wants no limit; `complete` and `totalReachable` always say what you did not get |
| `exclude` | array of string |  | files to leave out of the result (ones you already have). Still walked THROUGH, so anything reachable only via an excluded file still comes back |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

## `index_create`

Write a document that is a list of links to the given files — the way to turn a search or a query result into something durable you can come back to. The index is an ORDINARY FILE: in git, with a dot of its own, and its links become connectors, so it shows up in `graph_get` like anything else. It carries no summaries — those live on the dot, and a copy here would go stale on its own. Prune it by editing the file; `dot_get index=` and `file_read index=` read the file, so your edit is the answer. Refuses to replace an existing file unless overwrite=true. A path that is not a file is reported in `missing` and left out — one stale path never costs you the index.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `path` | string | yes | source-relative path to write the index at |
| `files` | array of string | yes | file paths or ids to list, in the order you want them |
| `title` | string |  | index title (default: derived from the filename) |
| `overwrite` | boolean |  | replace an existing file (default false) |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |


## `obsolescence_review`

React to a decision file: flag every note the kernel's general impact graph says it touches (`graph_affected`, embedding ∪ graph), judge each candidate with this plugin's configured engine, and stage confirmed corrections as unlanded commits on the `users/obsolescence` branch — the canonical checkout is never written to directly. The response says what happened: `candidates` lists everything flagged and why; `confirmed` lists the corrections actually staged, each with the judge's `reason`, `validUntil` and `score` (0–1 confidence, when the engine reported one); `branch` names the branch holding the staged commits, or `null` when nothing was confirmed. ## `property_get`

READ PROPERTIES off named files — the matching getter for `property_set`, and the context-cheapest way to ask "what is `owner` on these five files?". Name the files with `files`, or point `index` at a document and every file IT LINKS TO is the list; name the keys with `keys`, or omit it for the whole property bag. A requested key that is NOT on the dot is listed in `missing` rather than answered as null — "the value is nothing" and "the key is absent" are different facts, and reading one as the other is how a caller concludes an earlier write failed. THIS IS WHY TO PREFER IT OVER `dot_get fields=[…]`: that projection simply omits a key the dot does not carry, so `dot_get fields=["owner"]` on a file with no owner answers `{"path":"a.md"}` and you cannot tell an absent property from one you forgot to ask for. `property_list` is what tells you which keys EXIST to ask for.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `files` | array of string |  | file paths or ids. Over the CLI this is CWD-relative, exactly like `git add` — MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root (#337). |
| `index` | string |  | a document whose LINKS are the list of files — use instead of (or as well as) `files`. Any document works, not a special format: a generated index from `index_create`, or a hand-written note with links in prose. Read from the file every time, so pruning a line changes the answer. External URLs and dead links are skipped rather than reported missing. Over the CLI this is CWD-RELATIVE, exactly like git (#337); MCP and HTTP always take it relative to the source root. |
| `keys` | array of string |  | property keys to read (default: every property on the dot) |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

## `property_list`

This source's property vocabulary — what it DECLARES and what is actually in use, in one answer. READ THIS BEFORE `property_set`: each row gives the key, `origin`, `registered`, the declared `merge` and `description`, how many files carry it, the value types, and the `values` actually in use — which is what stops you inventing a synonym for a term the source already has. `origin` separates two populations that used to look identical: `source` means declared in this source's `.dotworld/properties.json`, so it is in git and travels with a clone and can be withdrawn by `property_unregister`; `built-in` means it ships with dotworld, is deliberately not in that file, and cannot. `values` is CAPPED and `distinctValues` always carries the true total beside it — when they differ you are looking at a sample, and long or structured values are counted but not listed. A registered property appears even at count 0, so you can read what a source allows before anyone has used it; an UNREGISTERED property in use appears with registered:false and no origin — real metadata, but nothing merges it and no write can target it until you `property_register` it. Pass `file` or `index` to scope the counts and values to those files ("what is on this") while still listing the whole declared vocabulary ("what may I write here"). Files whose dot cannot be parsed contribute NOTHING to these counts — the advisory beside the result names them.

## `property_register`

Declare a property in THIS source's registry (`.dotworld/properties.json`, durable and in git), so it can be written, targeted by commands, and merged by a strategy you chose. The registry is PER SOURCE: registering here licenses nothing in another source. Registering an existing name UPDATES it — that is how a source changes its mind — and the answer DISCLOSES what changed: when the merge strategy differs from the one that governed before, it carries `strategyChanged` (from → to) and `filesCarrying`, the number of dots already holding values the new strategy now governs (check those when changing shape: a scalar under `union` falls back to `last-writer`). Registering a name that ships with dotworld answers `overridesBuiltIn: true` — the override shadows the shipped declaration until `property_unregister` reverts it. An unchanged re-registration adds none of these fields. `merge` says how two writers editing the same property are reconciled: `last-writer` (scalars — a true divergence still conflicts), `union` (sets, with 3-way deletion tracking, so a removed element stays removed; a value that is not an ARRAY is not a set, so it falls back to `last-writer` the same way `line-union` does below), `line-union` (multi-line TEXT — both writers' lines are kept, with the same deletion tracking; this is how the dot body merges. It never conflicts ON TEXT, but a value that is NOT a string has no lines, so it falls back to `last-writer` and a true divergence on it still conflicts — do not read it as "this property can never block a land"), `counter` (ONE number, merged by SUMMING each side's own change against the merge base: a branch that left main at 5 and counted to 8 contributes +3, whichever order branches land in. Not a max and not a last-writer — those both answer 8 where 26 things happened. The value is a plain number, so `value=26` is the whole of it; a value that is not a finite number cannot be subtracted, so it falls back to `last-writer` like the two above, and that includes the per-actor `{actor: {count, lastReadAt}}` map that was this strategy's internal shape before #392 — sum the actors and write the total. Two limits worth knowing: a merge resolved from plain 2-way conflict markers has no trustworthy base, so it conflicts rather than inventing a total, and deleting the property on one side while the other counts on resurrects it at that side's delta). An UNREGISTERED property is never deleted or migrated — it stays on the file — but nothing merges it: a divergence on it conflicts and stays conflicted until someone registers it or settles the line by hand. `description` is required and is what tells the next reader (often a model) what the property is for.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `name` | string | yes | property name (may not be reserved dot frontmatter: id, source_id, title, tags, source_path) |
| `merge` | string | yes | merge strategy: last-writer \| union \| line-union \| counter |
| `description` | string | yes | what this property is for — served to agents as its meaning |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

A property is registered per source or it has no features. The registry is `.dotworld/properties.json` — durable and in git.

```console
$ dot property_register name=owner merge=last-writer 'description=the person accountable for this file'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "name": "owner",
    "merge": "last-writer",
    "description": "the person accountable for this file"
  }
}
```

## `property_set`

Set ONE dot property (metadata never touches the source file). `property_get` is the matching read. The key must be REGISTERED IN THIS WORKING TREE — `property_list` shows the vocabulary, `property_register` extends it. An unregistered key is refused with BAD_PARAMS, and the refusal distinguishes "already on this file but unregistered" from "not registered in this working tree": the first means the metadata exists and registering it adopts what is written; the second checks only THIS working tree's copy of the registry — another branch or workspace of the same source may already declare it, in which case pulling that change in (rather than re-registering here) is what resolves it. RESERVED DOT FRONTMATTER IS ALSO REFUSED — `title`, `tags`, `id`, `source_id`, `source_path` are not properties and do not live in the property bag, so writing one here would overwrite the dot's real field instead of storing a property (`key=tags value=5` used to DELETE a file's tags and report success). Use `dot_set` for `title` and `tags`; the identity fields are dotworld's and nothing may set them.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `file` | string | yes | file path |
| `key` | string | yes | property key. Must be registered — see `property_register`, and `property_list` for what this source already declares. May NOT be reserved dot frontmatter (title, tags, id, source_id, source_path): those are not properties and `property_register` refuses them too — `dot_set` is what writes `title` and `tags`. |
| `value` | any |  | property value (any JSON value: string, number, boolean, object, array, or null) |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

```console
$ dot property_set file=notes/retention.md key=owner value=alice
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "ok": true
  }
}
```

The refusal an unregistered property earns. Register it first, or the merge cannot know how to resolve two writers.

```console
$ dot property_set file=notes/retention.md key=reviewer value=bob
{
  "ok": false,
  "error": "`reviewer` is not registered in this working tree (source 'handbook'), and is on no dot there either. This only checks the registry on THIS working tree — another branch or workspace of the same source may already declare it; `property_list` there would show. Otherwise register it here first — `property_register name=reviewer merge=last-writer description='…'` — then set the value. `property_list` shows the vocabulary this working tree declares.",
  "code": "BAD_PARAMS"
}
```

## `property_unregister`

Withdraw a declaration from THIS source's registry — the counterpart to `property_register`. THE DATA STAYS: the property remains on every dot that carries it, because an unregistered property is never deleted or migrated. What it loses is its merge strategy and the ability to be targeted by a write, so `filesCarrying` in the answer tells you how much metadata just became unmergeable — learn it here rather than at a conflict. `property_unset` is what removes a property from a file. A BUILT-IN is refused: it ships with dotworld rather than living in `.dotworld/properties.json`, so there is nothing to take out (`property_list` marks each row `built-in` or `source`). Withdrawing a source OVERRIDE of a built-in works and reverts it to the shipped declaration.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `name` | string | yes | property name to withdraw (must be declared by this source) |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

Withdraws the declaration. Values already written to dots stay on the files — this is the vocabulary, not the data.

```console
$ dot property_unregister name=owner
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "name": "owner",
    "removed": {
      "merge": "last-writer",
      "description": "the person accountable for this file"
    },
    "revertedToBuiltIn": false,
    "filesCarrying": 0
  }
}
```

## `property_unset`

Remove a property from ONE dot. The source file is never touched, and no other property is. Removing a key that is not there is not an error — `removed: false` says the requested end state already held. AN UNREGISTERED KEY IS REMOVED TOO, by explicit request: #279 forbids the MERGE from deleting or migrating an unregistered property, because dotworld silently discarding metadata it has no strategy for is what the registry exists to prevent — but this is a caller naming a key, not an auto-resolution, and refusing would make `property_register` a required step towards deleting something. Reserved dot frontmatter (title, tags, …) is refused: it is not a property — use `dot_set`. Unsetting `summary` drops its `summary_hash` with it.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `file` | string | yes | file path |
| `key` | string | yes | property key to remove |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

```console
$ dot property_unset file=notes/retention.md key=owner
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "path": "notes/retention.md",
    "key": "owner",
    "removed": true,
    "wasRegistered": true
  }
}
```

## `search_grep`

Exact-string / identifier lookup — grep over files, always current. Binary files are skipped, as git's own grep skips them: they have no lines, and matching their utf8 decode returned a "line" of replacement characters from inside an image.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `pattern` | string | yes | regex pattern |
| `flags` | string |  | regex flags |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

```console
$ dot search_grep 'pattern=90 days'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": [
    {
      "path": "notes/retention.md",
      "line": 3,
      "text": "We keep customer event logs for 90 days, then delete them. Billing records are"
    }
  ]
}

ANSWERED FROM THE CANONICAL CHECKOUT — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```
