## `search_properties`

Find files by dot metadata — e.g. which files have owner=alice, which are over five hours, which are still untagged. EVERY criterion ANDs with the others; there is no OR. `where` takes exact values (`{"owner":"alice"}`, matched by value and never by stringification — 3 is not "3") and COMPARISONS, written as an operator object: `{"hours":{"gt":5},"status":{"ne":"done"}}`, with `eq` `ne` `gt` `gte` `lt` `lte`. Ordering compares numbers numerically and strings lexicographically, which is what sorts ISO dates; a comparison across types, or against a boolean/array/object/null, is REFUSED rather than silently dropped. A key the file does not carry matches `ne` and nothing else. A `where` value is read as operators only when ALL its keys are operator names, so a property whose real value is literally {"gt":5} cannot be queried. `hasKey`/`missingKey` ask whether a property is there at all; `hasTag`/`missingTag` ask the same of TAGS, which are frontmatter and not properties, so they never match a property criterion. `files` narrows the scan to a candidate set — feed it a `grep -rl` result — and on its own returns those files, which is the one way to get an answer with no property criteria at all. An EMPTY `files` answers `[]`: a grep that matched nothing leaves no candidates, so it cannot leave matches, and reading it as "no scope" would answer with the whole source. A file carrying dotUnparseable: true is returned REGARDLESS of the criteria: its metadata cannot be read, so whether it matches is unknown rather than false (`files` still bounds it — that is a scope, not a criterion). An UNREGISTERED key still matches — the data is the data — and the advisory beside the result says so, distinguishing a key that is on files but undeclared from one that is simply absent.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `where` | object |  | property criteria, ANDed. A plain value means equality; an operator object — every key one of eq/ne/gt/gte/lt/lte — means a comparison |
| `hasKey` | string |  | match files carrying this property key, whatever its value |
| `missingKey` | string |  | match files NOT carrying this property key |
| `hasTag` | string |  | match files carrying this tag |
| `missingTag` | string |  | match files NOT carrying this tag |
| `files` | array of string |  | restrict the scan to these file paths (a candidate set, e.g. from `grep -rl`); alone, it returns their dot metadata. An unindexed path is skipped, but a list where NONE resolve is refused; an empty list answers `[]` |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

```console
$ dot search_properties 'where={"owner":"alice"}'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": [
    {
      "id": "notes/retention.md",
      "sourceId": "handbook",
      "path": "notes/retention.md",
      "title": "Data retention policy",
      "tags": [
        "policy",
        "compliance"
      ],
      "dot": {
        "id": "notes/retention.md",
        "source_id": "handbook",
        "title": "Data retention policy",
        "tags": [
          "policy",
          "compliance"
        ],
        "source_path": "$DOTWORLD_ROOT/notes/retention.md",
        "properties": {
          "kind": "prose",
          "summary": "<!-- unread - summarize this file -->",
          "owner": "alice"
        },
        "body": "Reviewed each quarter by the data protection lead.\n"
      }
    }
  ]
}

ANSWERED FROM THE CANONICAL CHECKOUT — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```

## `search_semantic`

Discovery (agent-primary): turn a task into ranked candidate files. A hit carrying dotUnparseable: true has UNREADABLE metadata — its summary/summaryStatus are placeholders, not facts; do not read "unread" as "nobody summarised it". `obsolete`/`superseded` are stated on every hit — check them before reading: a superseded file can still rank above its replacement, and this is the only reliable way to tell (#355). The top of the ranking is reranked with lexical query/document overlap before `limit` is applied, which corrects a known failure mode where whole-document embedding leaves several candidates nearly tied — this narrows near-ties, it does not override a decisive semantic match. Refuses with BAD_PARAMS, rather than silently ranking on a weaker fallback, when dotworld.config.json names a specific embedding engine that could not be built — engine: "auto" degrades instead of refusing (see embedding_info, including `maxTokens`: a long document may be ranked on its opening section only).

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `query` | string | yes | the task / query text |
| `limit` | number |  | max results (default 10) |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

Ranked candidates, not answers. `score` is cosine similarity after the lexical rerank.

## `source_register`

Point the kernel at a repo directory as a source (one source = one repo). `root` MUST BE the repository's toplevel — a subdirectory of a repo is refused, and so is a directory that is not a git repository at all (use `initGit=true`, or `git init` it yourself, to make it one). A knowledge base living inside a larger project needs its own repository. THERE IS NO BRANCH TO REGISTER: dotworld holds no landing target (#396). A workspace forks from wherever the repo's canonical checkout has its HEAD, and `workspace_submit` merges back into that same checkout, wherever it is standing at the time. To change where work lands, `git checkout` there — `workspace_list` reports the canonical checkout and its branch.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | yes | source id |
| `root` | string | yes | absolute path to the source directory — must be a git repo's toplevel |
| `initGit` | boolean |  | initialise a git repo if absent. The branch name is git's own (`init.defaultBranch`, or whatever your git defaults to) — dotworld does not choose one |
| `neverPushDotworld` | boolean |  | When true, installs a git pre-push hook that strips every `.dotworld/**` path from history before anything reaches a remote — a plain `git push` from this source will never let dotworld's own metadata leave the machine; the raw push is rejected and a filtered equivalent is pushed in its place instead, automatically, with no dotworld command involved. The choice is written to `.dotworld/publish-policy.json` — durable and git-tracked — but note that it does NOT travel through a protected push: the policy file lives under `.dotworld/`, so the filter strips it along with everything else, and a remote fed only by filtered pushes never sees it. It reaches another machine by any route that copies the tree whole — a local clone, a copy, or a push made before the policy was turned on — and on those, that clone's next source_register installs the hook from the committed file with no action of its own. THE CLAIM IS NEVER WRITTEN UNLESS IT IS ENFORCED: the hook goes in first, and an explicit `true` that cannot be installed is REFUSED with the reason rather than recorded, because a durable file asserting a protection nothing enforces is worse than no protection. Pass `false` to remove the durable policy and uninstall dotworld's own hook; that direction needs no hook and always succeeds. A pre-push hook this did not install itself is NEVER touched, in either direction — installing refuses rather than overwriting it, and turning the policy off leaves a foreign hook exactly as it was. Omit this param entirely to leave the current policy untouched, including on the first `source_register` of an id — a repo dotworld has just met is pushable by default (#404: enforcing local-by-default meant the pre-push hook had to rewrite the caller's own push configuration, which corrupted it in ways worse than the protection was worth); pass `neverPushDotworld=true` explicitly to protect it. |

A repo dotworld has just met is pushable by default — `neverPushDotworld` is passed explicitly here to protect it.

```console
$ dot source_register id=handbook root=. neverPushDotworld=true
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "id": "handbook",
    "root": "/path/to/handbook",
    "publishPolicy": {
      "neverPushDotworld": true,
      "prePushHook": {
        "installed": true
      }
    }
  }
}
```

---

## `source_unregister`

Forget where a source lives — the inverse of `source_register`. THIS DELETES NOTHING ON DISK. A source root is your repository; unregistering is forgetting where it is, not removing it. Your files stay, and so does the `.dotworld/` directory inside them — the dots are durable, in git, and belong to the repo rather than to the registry, so registering the same root again brings every title, tag and property back. The disposable `.dotworld/derived/` index is left too, deliberately: a warm re-register is not worth giving the one command that destroys nothing a way to destroy something. The answer names the root, which is what you need to re-register, and `workspaces`: any workspaces this source has are NOT removed, and `workspace_close` needs a registered source, so close them first or you will have to re-register to reach them. A source DECLARED in `dotworld.config.json` is registered again on the next boot — remove the declaration, not just the registration.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | yes | the id of the source to forget |

Forgets where the source lives. THIS DELETES NOTHING in the repository — the files, the dots and the git history are all still there.

```console
$ dot source_unregister id=handbook
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "id": "handbook",
    "root": "/path/to/handbook",
    "workspaces": [],
    "stillVisible": false,
    "detail": "handbook is no longer registered. Nothing on disk was touched — re-register it with `source_register id=handbook root=/path/to/handbook` and its dots are still there."
  }
}
```

---

## `source_update`

Repoint a registered source at a different `root`. THIS EDITS THE REGISTRY, NOT THE TREES: nothing on disk moves, and the directory a source used to point at is left exactly as it was. Three refusals worth knowing: an id that is not registered is refused rather than created (this is not a second door to `source_register`), a `root` that does not exist is refused rather than created — a mistyped path would otherwise repoint a live source at an empty directory and every command would then answer, truthfully, that there is nothing there — and a `root` that is not a git repo's toplevel is refused, same as `source_register` (one source = one repo). `neverPushDotworld` alone is also a complete call on its own — it does not need `root` alongside it. There is no branch to repoint (#396): where work lands is what the canonical checkout has checked out, and `git checkout` is how you change it.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | yes | the id of the source to change |
| `root` | string |  | the new absolute path to the source directory (must already exist, and be a git repo's toplevel) |
| `neverPushDotworld` | boolean |  | When true, installs a git pre-push hook that strips every `.dotworld/**` path from history before anything reaches a remote — a plain `git push` from this source will never let dotworld's own metadata leave the machine; the raw push is rejected and a filtered equivalent is pushed in its place instead, automatically, with no dotworld command involved. The choice is written to `.dotworld/publish-policy.json` — durable and git-tracked — but note that it does NOT travel through a protected push: the policy file lives under `.dotworld/`, so the filter strips it along with everything else, and a remote fed only by filtered pushes never sees it. It reaches another machine by any route that copies the tree whole — a local clone, a copy, or a push made before the policy was turned on — and on those, that clone's next source_register installs the hook from the committed file with no action of its own. THE CLAIM IS NEVER WRITTEN UNLESS IT IS ENFORCED: the hook goes in first, and an explicit `true` that cannot be installed is REFUSED with the reason rather than recorded, because a durable file asserting a protection nothing enforces is worse than no protection. Pass `false` to remove the durable policy and uninstall dotworld's own hook; that direction needs no hook and always succeeds. A pre-push hook this did not install itself is NEVER touched, in either direction — installing refuses rather than overwriting it, and turning the policy off leaves a foreign hook exactly as it was. Omit this param entirely to leave the current policy untouched, including on the first `source_register` of an id — a repo dotworld has just met is pushable by default (#404: enforcing local-by-default meant the pre-push hook had to rewrite the caller's own push configuration, which corrupted it in ways worse than the protection was worth); pass `neverPushDotworld=true` explicitly to protect it. |

Turning the publish policy OFF needs no hook and always succeeds. After this, a plain `git push` may carry `.dotworld/`.

```console
$ dot source_update id=handbook neverPushDotworld=false
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "id": "handbook",
    "root": "/path/to/handbook",
    "publishPolicy": {
      "neverPushDotworld": false,
      "prePushHook": {
        "removed": true
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## `summary_refresh`

Rewrite the summaries that no longer describe their file, for the files you name. A summary is stale when the body changed after it was written (`summary_hash`, the same comparison `dot_get`'s `summaryStatus` reports) — the kernel detects that and has no opinion about what the summary should now say, because the kernel holds no model; this plugin asks its engine. Name what to refresh with `files` (paths, a directory like `docs/`, or `*` for the whole source), `index` (a document whose links are the list), or both — the index is appended after the files and deduped. A name that is both a file and a directory resolves to the FILE, because identity is the path. Naming NEITHER refuses: there is no default, because the default would be rewriting every dot in the source. It REFRESHES, it does not author: a file with no summary yet (an `unread` placeholder) is left alone, and so is one whose summary is still current — naming a file asks for a refresh-if-stale, not an unconditional rewrite. Writes go straight to the dots in the working tree, uncommitted, and a rewritten summary is re-stamped against the body it now describes, so the file reads `current` and is not re-drafted next time. `refreshed` reports each one with the summary it replaced; review with `git diff` and commit them like any other edit. Nothing is branched, queued or committed on your behalf. A stale file whose redraft comes back IDENTICAL to the summary already there is reported in `reverified`, not `refreshed`: the text is left alone and only the stamp is rewritten, recording that the engine read this body and confirmed it — so the file converges to `current` instead of being re-drafted, and paid for, on every later call. One file failing — a model that times out, a dot that will not parse, an engine that answers with nothing — does not abandon the rest: it lands in `failed` with its error, the run continues, that file stays stale so a later call retries it, and every path in `refreshed` was really written.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL. Omitted, dotworld infers it from your working directory (your own workspace counts), exactly like every other command's sourceId. |
| `files` | array of string |  | what to refresh — use instead of (or as well as) `index`. Four spellings, and they mix freely in one list: a file path (`"runbooks/deploy.md"`); a DIRECTORY, with or without a trailing slash (`"docs/"`), which selects the files under it; `"*"`, which selects the whole source; and a list of any of those. There is deliberately no separate `all` param — `"*"` is the spelling for the whole corpus. Over the CLI these are CWD-relative, exactly like `git add` (so `"*"` typed from a subdirectory means that subdirectory); MCP and HTTP always take them relative to the source root. A path that resolves to nothing is REPORTED in `missing`, never a refusal — the rest of the list is still refreshed. |
| `index` | string |  | a document whose LINKS are the list of files to refresh — use instead of (or as well as) `files`. Any document works: a generated index from `index_create`, or a hand-written note with links in prose. Read from the file every call, so pruning a line changes what gets refreshed, exactly like `file_read index=` / `context_load index=`. |
| `recursive` | boolean |  | does a DIRECTORY selection descend into subdirectories? Default true. Applies to `"*"` too, which is the source root as a directory: `files=["*"] recursive=false` refreshes only the files at the top level. No effect on a file named directly, or on `index`'s links. |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to write to (default: the canonical checkout — see `property_set`'s `workspace` param, which this matches exactly). The dots are written here and left uncommitted: `git diff` is the review, and you commit them like any other edit. |

```console
$ dot summary_refresh 'files=["notes/incident-2026-03.md"]'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "selected": 1,
    "refreshed": [],
    "reverified": [],
    "skipped": {
      "stillCurrent": 0,
      "unstamped": 1
    },
    "failed": [],
    "missing": []
  }
}
```

## `sync_doctor`

Is this install silently half-working? One call, every condition dotworld can be broken in without saying so: a merge driver that is registered but NOT RUNNABLE (reading the config key cannot tell — this RUNS it, the way git does, on synthetic files in a temp directory), a second driver registered under another name, an embedding engine that fell back, absent model weights, a build behind its source, a registered source whose root is gone, stranded dots, dots describing a file that is HERE and gitignored (so nothing indexes it and its metadata is in no answer — reported with the rule that excluded it, and separately from the stranded ones, because the repair is neither of theirs), dots that will not parse, titles naming a file that has been renamed away, authored edges pointing at nothing, connector files that will not parse or hold a weight the graph cannot use (each named with its reason — they are skipped silently otherwise, absent from graph_get and from every centrality score), worktree registrations orphaned by an rm -rf, an UNRESOLVED MERGE CONFLICT anywhere in the source (asked of git directly — every other check here reads files on disk and cannot tell a conflicted path from a settled one), durable state under .dotworld/ (properties.json, connectors) that differs from what is committed — the same silent gap `rm -rf .dotworld` leaves even after `sync_source` re-mints blank dots — and a dot present on disk but never committed. Machine-wide: it takes no sourceId, because "is my install healthy" is not a question whose answer should change with your working directory — every check here holds that except two. The search-engine and model-weights checks report on whichever `dotworld.config.json` this PROCESS resolved (DOTWORLD_PLUGIN_CONFIG, else the machine config dir, else cwd — docs/plugins.md), so on a machine with no config in the machine config dir the answer follows the caller's cwd like every other cwd-resolved read. Both checks name the file (or say none was found) in their `detail`, so which config produced the answer is always stated rather than implied. Every check reports one of ok / warn / fail / unknown / skipped, and 'unknown' — a check that could not be ESTABLISHED — keeps `ok` false, because a green verdict nobody established is the silent half-working this exists to end. `notChecked` names what it deliberately does not cover. It is a READ: no staging, no `git config <key> <value>`, no indexing, no workspace created. `repair=true` is the only thing that writes, and only for the two repairs that re-assert state dotworld itself wrote — re-registering the merge driver and `git worktree prune`. Everything else reports the command to run and touches nothing.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `repair` | boolean |  | ALSO write the two repairs dotworld owns: re-register the merge driver, and prune worktree registrations whose directory is gone. Default false — a diagnostic that mutates on first run cannot be used to diagnose. Never repairs anything a human has to decide (a stranded dot may hold the only copy of some metadata) and never rewrites a line in your attributes file or a merge.* section it did not write. The report shows what was FOUND; re-run without the flag to confirm the fix. |

```console
$ dot sync_doctor
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "ok": false,
    "status": "warn",
    "sources": [
      "handbook"
    ],
    "checks": [
      {
        "id": "build",
        "scope": "machine",
        "status": "ok",
        "detail": "dist/ matches src/ (built <varies>, rev <varies>)."
      },
      {
        "id": "search-engine",
        "scope": "machine",
        "status": "ok",
        "detail": "Search is running on 'fastembed', exactly as configured ('fastembed'). Config file in effect for this process: /path/to/handbook/.dotworld/dotworld.config.json."
      },
      {
        "id": "model-weights",
        "scope": "machine",
        "status": "ok",
        "detail": "Weights for 'fast-all-MiniLM-L6-v2' are present in /home/dragonlord/.cache/dotworld/models. Config file in effect for this process: /path/to/handbook/.dotworld/dotworld.config.json."
      },
      {
        "id": "source-roots",
        "scope": "machine",
… 100 more lines of output
```

## `sync_merge`

REPAIR: re-merge dots per property that a plain `git merge` left unreconciled. Use it when a merge reported CONFLICT on a `.dot.md`, or when `dot_get` answers dotUnparseable: true. Name the FILES with `files`; omit it and every dot in the tree that needs it is found. Accepts any path and never refuses on a settled tree — this is a repair tool, not a merge-in-progress helper. It writes the reconciled dot and STAGES NOTHING: accepting the result is your own explicit `file_stage` or `git add`. Note that a dot damaged by a driver that FAILED carries no conflict markers at all — git leaves it well-formed with only one side in it — so "the file looks fine" is not evidence there is nothing to repair. READ THE `outcome` OF EVERY ROW — it does not all mean the same thing. `merged` = settled and written. `conflicts` = a property changed on both sides with no strategy to settle it. On route `index` THE DOT WAS STILL WRITTEN, and a side won: a registered scalar keeps THEIRS, an unregistered property keeps OURS. `detail` names which properties and which side, and you should read it before you `git add` — that is the moment the winner becomes permanent. On route `markers` nothing is written at all and the file is left EXACTLY as it is, markers and all, because that block is the only surviving copy of the other side. `delete-conflict` = git reports the dot unmerged as a MODIFY/DELETE — one branch deleted it, the other edited it — so there is no second version to merge and nothing was written; `detail` says which side deleted and gives the two commands that settle it. `nothing-to-merge` = nothing was repaired, and is NOT success: a writer who already resolved a failed merge by staging their own side looks identical, and the side they dropped survives only in the merge commit's parents, which this does not read. `route` and `base` say how good the answer is: route `index` takes all three sides from git's index (base `real`, a full 3-way); route `markers` recovers them from the conflict markers in the file, and its base is `reconstructed` — every line outside the contested hunks — unless you run `merge.conflictStyle=diff3`, which puts the true base in the file and makes it `real`. A reconstructed base still unions tags correctly; what it cannot do is tell "both sides changed this scalar" from "the base never had it", so such a property conflicts rather than being guessed.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `files` | array of string |  | file paths whose dots to re-merge (default: every dot in the tree that needs it) |
| `workspace` | string |  | working tree to act in (default: yours — see workspace_open). Under a declared auth mode this is still honoured verbatim: naming another identity's workspace path routes the write into THAT identity's branch, not yours, regardless of who is authenticated — an explicit workspace outranks identity, by design (docs/multi-user.md, R21). Only pass a path you opened yourself or were handed. |

REPAIR: re-merge dots per property where a plain `git merge` left conflict markers. Ordinary submits do this for you — this is the door back in when a merge happened outside dotworld.

```console
$ dot sync_merge
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": []
}
```

## `sync_source`

Rebuild the disposable index for a source from the files of ONE working tree, and MINT: write a blank dot for every file that has none, and heal a `kind` written before #255. This is the one bulk-mint dotworld still does (#383) — every read command answers from an in-memory row and writes nothing, so a dotless file stays dotless on disk until this runs. The index is per tree (#268), so this rebuilds the tree it resolves — pass `workspace` to rebuild a workspace rather than the canonical checkout. Rebuilding also reconciles out-of-band renames: in a GIT source, a file you moved with `mv` or `git mv` keeps its dot — title, tags and properties — even if you edited it in the same sitting, both before and after you commit the move, and whether the source is the repository root or a directory inside it. Reconciliation itself runs on every read, not only here — you need not call this after moving a file for that part. In a NON-GIT source only an unedited move is followed, because the content hash is the only evidence available. Where a move cannot be identified — too heavy a rewrite, an edited move outside git, or a move whose destination is outside THIS source (a file moved out of the tree has no destination here to carry a dot onto) — nothing is guessed: the moved file is described by a blank dot (this command writes it; a plain read answers with an equivalent one without saving it) and the old dot is left behind holding the real metadata. `dot_list orphaned=true` is where those leftovers are, with what each one holds and where git suggests the file went, and `dot_attach` reattaches one — so a file whose metadata came back empty after a move is a recovery, not a re-authoring. An advisory beside this answer counts them when there are any, because these counts are of live files and say nothing about a stranded dot.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `workspace` | string |  | The working tree to answer from. THE INDEX IS PER WORKING TREE: this answer describes ONE tree, so two writers legitimately get different results, rankings, importance and read counts for the same query. OMITTING THIS DOES NOT MEAN "MY WORKSPACE": with no declared auth mode you are not routed to one, and the answer comes from the canonical checkout — where your own unlanded work is simply absent. Call `workspace_list` to see the workspaces that exist and pass one of their paths here; `workspace_open` creates yours if you have none. Whichever tree answers, an advisory beside the result names it and names any workspace it could not see. |

Rebuilds the disposable index and mints a `.dot.md` for every file that lacks one. A file added by hand is invisible to dotworld until this runs.

```console
$ dot sync_source sourceId=handbook
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "files": 4,
    "connectors": 2
  }
}
```

## `version`

Which build is answering you, which search engine it is running, and which commands it serves. Returns { build, node, engine, commands, note }. `build.stale: true` means the running build is behind its source and every face is serving old code — rebuild (npm run build); `build.stale: null` means freshness is NOT KNOWABLE here (running from source, or an installed package with no src/ to compare against) and must not be read as fresh. `commands` is the command set itself, so a client written against an older set can ask directly whether what it needs is still served rather than discovering it one UNKNOWN_COMMAND at a time. For whether the install is HEALTHY — merge driver, stranded dots, dead worktree registrations — ask sync_doctor.

_No parameters._

## `workspace_close`

Remove a workspace — the inverse of `workspace_open`. YOUR BRANCH SURVIVES: the worktree is taken down through git (`worktree remove` then `prune`, never `rm -rf`), and `users/<name>` is deliberately left alone, so commits you have not landed are still there and `workspace_submit` still lands them — a land needs a BRANCH, not a worktree. It refuses exactly ONE thing: UNCOMMITTED changes, which are on no branch, which `git worktree remove` deletes, and which nothing could bring back. `force=true` overrides that and discards them. UNLANDED COMMITS are not refused (#394) — they are not loss, the branch keeps them, `workspace_submit` still lands them with no worktree in existence, and `git subcommand=branch flags=--no-merged` finds the branch again — so they are REPORTED: `unlanded` counts them and `detail` says what that count means. UNLANDED RELATIVE TO WHAT: the branch the canonical checkout has checked out right now, which `detail` names (#396). Read `detail` when `unlanded` is non-zero — the number measures ANCESTRY, so a squash-land leaves it non-zero about work that is already in, and `detail` says so. A removal git declines (a locked worktree, a permission failure) is an error, never a success — this never reports `closed` for a directory still on disk. `workspace_list` shows every working tree, of which the `managed` ones are what this closes; reopening one recreates the worktree on the same branch, with its history intact.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `as` | string |  | close a workspace opened under a name (auth mode `none` ONLY, mirroring `workspace_open`; refused under a declared auth mode, where your workspace is routed by your authenticated identity and naming another one would let you close one that is not yours) |
| `force` | boolean |  | DISCARD uncommitted changes and close anyway (default false). That is the only thing it overrides and the only thing it costs: no branch holds those bytes, so nothing can bring them back. Unlanded commits never needed it — they are reported, not refused (#394) |

Removes the worktree. The branch survives — closing a workspace is not throwing work away.

```console
$ dot workspace_close as=bob
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "name": "bob",
    "branch": "users/bob",
    "path": "/path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob",
    "closed": true,
    "branchKept": true,
    "unlanded": 0,
    "discarded": 0,
    "detail": "The workspace directory is gone; users/bob is not. It had nothing main does not already have."
  }
}
```

## `workspace_list`

EVERY working tree of this source — the answer comes from `git worktree list`, so it is every tree git knows about and not only the ones dotworld created (#395). Each carries its `branch` (git's answer, `null` on a detached HEAD), `path`, and what is IN it: `dirty` (uncommitted files) and `unlanded` (commits its branch has that the CANONICAL CHECKOUT does not — measured against whatever that checkout has checked out at the moment you ask, which is where `workspace_submit` merges, #396). `kind` says what you may DO with it. `managed` came from `workspace_open` and is the only kind `workspace_close` closes. `external` is a worktree made out of band — with plain `git worktree add`, very often by another agent's harness — which you can READ and target with `workspace=` but not close here. `canonical` is the source's own checkout, listed because its uncommitted work is exactly what `workspace_submit` refuses on as `tracked-checkout-dirty` and it is very often your own. `locked` and `prunable` are git's own words when it has them: locked means a close will be declined, prunable means the registration points at a directory that is gone. Worktrees live OUTSIDE the source root (#266), so `ls` in the notes folder cannot see them and this is how you find them. Use it to see whether the work you are looking for is in another tree — including one opened from a different FACE, since under auth mode `none` the CLI is user `local` and the MCP server is user `mcp`, so they are on different branches by default. To then SEE that work, pass its path as `workspace` to `git` (`status`, `diff`, `log`); to build on it without waiting for them to land, its branch is an ordinary ref — `git subcommand=merge ref=<branch>` — because linked worktrees share one repository.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |

```console
$ dot workspace_list
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": [
    {
      "name": "source",
      "branch": "main",
      "path": "/path/to/handbook",
      "kind": "canonical",
      "dirty": 0,
      "unlanded": 0
    },
    {
      "name": "bob",
      "branch": "users/bob",
      "path": "/path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob",
      "kind": "managed",
      "dirty": 0,
      "unlanded": 0
    }
  ]
}
```

## `workspace_open`

Create (or report) the calling user's isolated workspace on their own branch. ISOLATION IS A PROPERTY OF AUTHENTICATED DEPLOYMENTS: under auth mode `none` there is one identity, so every caller shares one workspace unless it names one with `as` — two agents on one no-auth server otherwise write to the same tree while each believes it is isolated. Note also that the identity differs by FACE under mode `none` (the CLI defaults to the identity of the workspace worktree its cwd is standing in, else `local`; the MCP server is `mcp`), so work opened on one face is on a branch the other does not look at; `branch` in the result is how you find out which. Whatever you get, thread the returned `workspace` path through every subsequent mutating call — nothing routes you there automatically without a declared auth mode.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `as` | string |  | name a workspace of your own (auth mode `none` ONLY; refused under a declared auth mode). It names a WORKSPACE, NOT AN IDENTITY: commits in it are still authored as the single local user, so `git log --author=<name>` will not find them. A deployment that wants isolation WITH attribution configures auth instead. |

An isolated worktree on `users/bob`, outside the source root. Bob works there; nobody edits the canonical checkout out from under him.

```console
$ dot workspace_open as=bob
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "path": "/path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob",
    "branch": "users/bob",
    "created": true
  }
}
```

---

## `workspace_submit`

Merge the calling user's branch INTO THE CANONICAL CHECKOUT, wherever it is standing. dotworld holds no landing target (#396): it resolves nothing, checks nothing out, and never moves your HEAD — it merges where you are and reports `target`, the branch it merged into (git's own `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`, so a detached checkout reads `HEAD`). To land somewhere else, `git checkout` there first. Divergence is reported the way GIT reports it and nothing more: status 'blocked' with blockedBy.reason 'needs-rebase' and the conflicted PATHS. There is no per-field conflict payload and nothing to submit back — resolve it in your own workspace, exactly as a shell user would: `git rebase`, read the marked file with file_read, send the reconciled text with file_stage, then `git rebase --continue` and workspace_submit again. Refused with blockedBy.reason 'dot-unparseable' when the branch carries a .dot.md dotworld cannot read (e.g. committed merge markers). EVERY refusal carries blockedBy.detail: one sentence naming the cause and the way out, and stating explicitly that nothing was landed and nothing was written — so re-running once you have acted on it is safe. Read it before touching the checkout: 'tracked-checkout-dirty' means the shared checkout holds UNCOMMITTED WORK, which is very often your own, and clearing it destroys the edits you were trying to submit. 'workspace-dirty' is the same hazard about YOUR OWN workspace (#370): dotworld never commits on your behalf, so uncommitted edits sitting there at the moment you submit are refused rather than silently left off the land — commit them (`git subcommand=commit`) and submit again. A resubmit of a branch the target already contains answers status 'up-to-date' with reason 'already-contained' (not a second 'merged' with a stale-looking commit hash, #357) — 'contained', not 'landed', because what contains it is `target` and `target` moves with your checkout. An untracked `.dot.md` — blank or authored — blocks like any other uncommitted path (#383): a read never mints one for you any more, so if one is sitting there it is real, and `git subcommand=rebase` never clears it out of the way either — commit it (`git subcommand=add` then `git subcommand=commit`) and submit again. A verdict carries `mediatedBy` only when a submit-wrapping plugin was attached, and it is PROVENANCE — the id of the plugin this call was dispatched to. It does not mean that plugin changed anything: the kernel performs the merge either way, and one that scanned, found nothing to do and did no work at all is stamped identically (#389). Absent means no wrapping plugin was attached. Whatever else such a plugin did, it did in git — look for it with `git subcommand=branch`, not in this answer.

| Param | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourceId` | string |  | source id — OPTIONAL for a caller with a working directory. The CLI infers it from your working directory, the way git infers the repository: a subdirectory works, and so does your own workspace (which lives outside the source root). A face with no working directory (this MCP server, or HTTP) can't infer one and refuses without it — pass it explicitly. Also pass it explicitly when you are outside every registered source, when two sources claim the same directory, or to act on a source you are not standing in. `source_list` names them. |
| `message` | string |  | land message |

Both sides edited the same lines. The conflict is reported the way git reports one — status plus the conflicted **paths**. dotworld never hands back a per-field payload with both sides in it; you settle it in your own workspace.

```console
$ dot workspace_submit 'message=retention: shorten the log window'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "status": "blocked",
    "blockedBy": {
      "reason": "needs-rebase",
      "paths": [
        "notes/retention.md"
      ],
      "generated": [],
      "detail": "Your branch has diverged from `main` on these paths. Nothing was landed and nothing was written. Resolve it where a shell user would — in your workspace: rebase onto it (`dot git subcommand=rebase ref=main`), read the marked file with `file_read`, send the reconciled text with `file_stage`, then continue the rebase and `workspace_submit` again. If git refuses the rebase citing an untracked `.dotworld/dots/*.dot.md` file, that dot is real uncommitted work: no read ever mints one any more, and nothing clears one out of the way for you (#383) — commit it (`git subcommand=add` then `git subcommand=commit`) or set it aside with `git subcommand=stash`, never delete it, then retry."
    }
  }
}

ANSWERED FROM THE WORKSPACE /path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```

With every conflicted path settled, the submit lands in the canonical checkout.

```console
$ dot workspace_submit 'message=retention: settle the log window at 90 days'
{
  "ok": true,
  "result": {
    "status": "merged",
    "commit": "7bbf0303446e5bc12ac19a3e2b59fd7e0e83fe85",
    "branch": "users/bob",
    "target": "main"
  }
}

ANSWERED FROM THE WORKSPACE /path/to/state/dotworld/worktrees/handbook/bob — resolved from your current directory, not from anything you passed. Pass `workspace=<path>` (see `workspace_list`) to choose a different tree explicitly.
```
